content:
A student I coach once burned four minutes on 3(x − 4) = 15. She distributed, doubted a sign, then started over twice. The algebra was easy; her order of steps was not. That is the real lesson of this SAT Math Linear Equations practice test. These questions rarely test hard ideas. They test whether you move in a clean, repeatable order under time pressure. Scroll down for 15 Digital SAT-style MCQs with instant scoring and full worked answers.

What the Digital SAT wants from linear equations

Most items here live in one variable. So you isolate x, and you do it fast. But the SAT hides the algebra inside stories, formulas and both-sides messes. Here is what shows up again and again:

  • Both-sides equations, where variables sit on the left and the right.
  • Fraction coefficients that beg to be cleared first.
  • Literal equations, where you solve for one letter among many.
  • Word problems that hide a simple equation inside a sentence.
  • The special cases: no solution, and infinitely many solutions.

Three habits behind this SAT Math Linear Equations practice test

You do not need more tricks. You need three habits. First, clear fractions before anything else; multiply every term by the lowest common denominator. Second, gather the variable on one side and the numbers on the other, then divide last. Third, read the special cases straight off the coefficients. That third habit saves the most time on this SAT Math Linear Equations practice test.

Clear the fractions first

Take (x)/(3) + (x)/(4) = 7. The denominators are 3 and 4, so multiply every term by 12. That gives 4x + 3x = 84, and then 7x = 84. So x = 12. No fiddly fractions, and no lost minus signs. One multiply, and the mess is gone.

Read the special cases off the coefficients

Say ax + 5 = 3x − 7. If a equals 3, the x-terms cancel and you are left with 5 = −7. That is false, so there is no solution. But if both sides became identical instead, every x would work, and you would have infinitely many solutions. You can spot both before you solve.

Traps that quietly cost marks

Careless order, not hard maths, sinks most scores here. So watch these three:

Question saysWeak moveStrong move
3(x − 4) = 5(x + 2) − 4xSolve before distributingDistribute both sides, then collect x
(x)/(3) + (x)/(4) = 7Cross-multiply piece by pieceMultiply every term by 12 at once
Solve for m in y = mx + bSubtract m from somewhereSubtract b, then divide by x

A quick worked example

Try 3(x − 4) = 5(x + 2) − 4x. Distribute first: 3x − 12 = 5x + 10 − 4x. The right side tidies to x + 10. So 3x − 12 = x + 10. Now subtract x, then add 12: 2x = 22. So x = 11. Notice the order never changed. Distribute, collect, divide, done. Every question on this SAT Math Linear Equations practice test rewards that same order.

Here is the caveat coaches rarely say aloud. A calculator does not help much on these. The Digital SAT lets you use one throughout, yet a linear equation is won or lost at the setup. Type in a wrong arrangement, and you get a confident wrong answer. So slow down for one breath before you solve.

What score to aim for

Set a simple bar: 12 out of 15 or better. If you land below 9, do not push ahead. Go back to the three habits above, redo the ones you missed, and retake the test in two days. That short gap matters, because spaced practice sticks far better than one long grind.

quiz.title: SAT Math Linear Equations Quiz
quiz.intro: Fifteen Digital SAT-style questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: The sum of two numbers is 30. If one number is twice the other, what is the smaller number?
questions.explanation: Let x represent the smaller number and 2x represent the larger number. The sum of the two numbers is given by x + 2x = 30. Combine like terms: 3x = 30. Divide both sides by 3: x = 10.

questions.q: Solve for m: y = mx + b
questions.explanation: To solve for m in the slope-intercept form of a linear equation y = mx + b, first subtract b from both sides to isolate the term containing m: y - b = mx. Next, divide both sides by x to solve for m: m = (y - b)/(x).

questions.q: The volume of a rectangular prism is V = lwh. Solve for h.
questions.explanation: To isolate h in the volume formula V = lwh, divide both sides by the product lw: h = (V)/(lw).

questions.q: If 3(x - 4) = 5(x + 2) - 4x, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Distribute: 3x - 12 = 5x + 10 - 4x. Simplify: 3x - 12 = x + 10. Subtract x from both sides: 2x - 12 = 10. Add 12 to both sides: 2x = 22. Divide by 2: x = 11.

questions.q: For what value of k does the equation 4(x - 3) + kx = 2(3x - 6) - 2x have infinitely many solutions?
questions.explanation: Expand both sides: 4x - 12 + kx = 6x - 12 - 2x, which simplifies to (4+k)x - 12 = 4x - 12. For infinitely many solutions the two sides must be identical, so 4 + k = 4, giving k = 0. Check: with k = 0 both sides equal 4x - 12.

questions.q: A pump can drain a tank in 12 hours. A second pump can drain the same tank in 8 hours. If both pumps work together, how long will it take to drain the tank?
questions.explanation: Let t be the time. The rate of pump 1 is 1/12 tank/hour. Rate of pump 2 is 1/8 tank/hour. Combined rate is 1/12 + 1/8 = 2/24 + 3/24 = 5/24. Set (5/24)t = 1. t = 24/5 = 4.8.

questions.q: If -4x = 28, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: To solve the equation -4x = 28, we need to isolate x by dividing both sides by -4. This operation yields x = (28)/(-4) = -7.

questions.q: If 3(x - 4) = 15, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: To solve 3(x - 4) = 15, we can use the distributive property or divide first. Dividing both sides by 3 gives x - 4 = 5. Then, add 4 to both sides to isolate x: x = 9.

questions.q: On a number line, point A is at 1 and point B is at 7. If point C is located such that its distance from A is twice its distance from B, which of the following could be the coordinate of C?
questions.explanation: Let x represent the coordinate of point C. The distance from A is |x - 1| and the distance from B is |x - 7|. The condition given in the problem translates to the equation |x - 1| = 2|x - 7|.
Distribute both sides: 2x + 3 = 3x - 2. Subtract 2x from both sides: 3 = x - 2. Add 2 to both sides: x = 5. Check: left side 0.25(40+12)=0.25(52)=13; right side 0.5(30-4)=0.5(26)=13. So x=5.

questions.q: Solve for c: ax + bc = d
questions.explanation: To isolate c in the equation ax + bc = d, first subtract ax from both sides to move the term not containing c to the other side: bc = d - ax. Next, divide both sides by b to solve for c: c = (d - ax)/(b).

questions.q: The Celsius to Fahrenheit conversion is F = (9)/(5)C + 32. Solve for C.
questions.explanation: To solve for C in the temperature conversion formula F = (9)/(5)C + 32, first subtract 32 from both sides: F - 32 = (9)/(5)C. Next, multiply both sides by the reciprocal of (9)/(5), which is (5)/(9): C = (5)/(9)(F - 32).
Find the common denominator (12): 4x/12 + 3x/12 = 7. 7x/12 = 7. Multiply by 12: 7x = 84. x = 12.

questions.q: Given the equation ax + 5 = 3x - 7, which of the following values of a results in an equation with no solution?
questions.explanation: For no solution, the variable terms must cancel while the constants remain unequal. If a=3, we get 3x + 5 = 3x - 7, which simplifies to 5 = -7. Since this is a contradiction, there is no solution.

questions.q: A merchant sells an item for 180 after a 25% discount. What was the original price of the item?
questions.explanation: Let x be the original price. The sale price is x - 0.25x = 0.75x. 0.75x = 180. x = 180 / 0.75 = 240.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to solve a both-sides equation?
faq.a: Distribute first, then collect every x on one side and every number on the other. Divide only at the very end. That order stops most sign errors.

faq.q: How do I spot no solution or infinitely many solutions?
faq.a: Simplify until the x-terms line up. If they cancel and the numbers disagree, there is no solution. If both sides are identical, there are infinitely many.

faq.q: Can I use a calculator on these questions?
faq.a: You can, since the Digital SAT allows one on all of Math. Still, set the equation up by hand first; a wrong arrangement gives a confident wrong answer.
